title: MQSS-Selector: RL-Guided Pass Selection for an MLIR Compilation Pipeline
summary: High Performance Computing (HPC) and Quantum Computing (QC) systems are increasingly converging towards unified High Performance Computing-Quantum Computing (HPCQC) infrastructures, driven by a growing need to bridge classical and quantum workflows, which affects all levels of the system stack, from the hardware to compilers and runtimes, all the way to applications. However, today's QC devices are still in the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era, are error-prone and resource-limited, and therefore require specialized optimizations and topology mappings to achieve sufficient fidelity. This places special emphasis on proper compilation and optimization within the overall quantum software stack. Many existing stacks remain fragmented, with separate components responsible for device selection, compiler-pass optimization, and job queue scheduling. This paper proposes a unified, learning-based selector that integrates these disparate stages into a cohesive framework. Our proposed selector scheme leverages reinforcement learning and deep learning models that can be extended to simultaneously optimize multiple objectives -- such as fidelity, compilation time, and scheduling latency -- while dynamically adapting to circuit characteristics and device conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a unified, learning-based selector that integrates device selection, compiler-pass optimization, and job queue scheduling into a single cohesive framework for HPCQC infrastructures, using reinforcement learning and deep learning to simultaneously optimize fidelity, compilation time, and scheduling latency while adapting dynamically to circuit and device conditions.
AI.motivation: HPC and QC systems are converging into unified HPCQC infrastructures, affecting the entire system stack from hardware to applications. However, NISQ-era QC devices are error-prone and resource-limited, requiring specialized optimizations and topology mappings to reach sufficient fidelity. Existing quantum software stacks remain fragmented, with separate components handling device selection, compiler-pass optimization, and job queue scheduling, which limits overall efficiency.
AI.method: The authors propose a unified, learning-based selector that merges previously disparate stages—device selection, compiler-pass optimization, and job queue scheduling—into one cohesive framework. The selector leverages reinforcement learning and deep learning models and can be extended to optimize multiple objectives simultaneously while adapting dynamically to circuit characteristics and device conditions.
AI.result: As this is a proposal abstract, no empirical results are reported. The claimed capability is a unified selector that can simultaneously optimize multiple objectives—fidelity, compilation time, and scheduling latency—while dynamically adapting to circuit characteristics and device conditions.
AI.conclusion: A unified, learning-based selector is proposed to overcome the fragmentation of current quantum software stacks, integrating device selection, compiler-pass optimization, and scheduling into a single RL/DL-driven framework for HPCQC infrastructures. This positions learning-based, multi-objective optimization as a path toward more cohesive and adaptive quantum compilation and resource management.

title: Learning and interpreting policies for simultaneous entanglement requests in quantum networks
summary: Future quantum networks will make use of entanglement to perform numerous tasks, such as sending quantum information over long distances, distributed quantum computing, and quantum sensing. In general, these tasks will need to be performed simultaneously in various regions of a network, while minimizing resources and latency. We will thus require policies for scheduling link-level entanglement resources, and using the link-level entanglement to create various forms of multipartite entanglement required for every task. In this work, we address this problem using reinforcement learning. We formulate a Markov Decision Process for the problem and use double deep Q-networks (DQN) with Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs), experience replay buffers, and curriculum training to obtain policies. The key physical parameter is the probability of link-level entanglement generation, i.e., the link activation probability. We show that our policies maintain 100% success for up to 71% lower link activation probability than the baseline heuristics for a set of physically relevant network topologies. We then examine an additional constraint where experiment (task) placements are restricted to specific hardware types and demonstrate a similar advantage in performance over heuristics, with our policy maintaining at least an 80% success rate for up to a 59% lower link activation probability. Finally, we explore methods to interpret the learned policy by defining metrics enabling conclusions to be drawn about the model's behavior and by tasking a large language model (LLM) to derive a novel heuristic given example actions taken by the DQN-trained policy. We find that the LLM heuristic performs similarly to the DQN-trained policy in performance, indicating a promising method for interpretable policy extraction for large quantum networks, where direct training becomes computationally expensive.

AI.tldr: This work uses reinforcement learning (double DQN with MPNNs) to schedule link-level entanglement and generate multipartite entanglement in quantum networks, achieving 100% success at up to 71% lower link activation probability than heuristics, and extracts interpretable policies via an LLM.
AI.motivation: Future quantum networks must perform multiple tasks (long-distance quantum information transfer, distributed quantum computing, quantum sensing) simultaneously across regions while minimizing resources and latency, requiring policies for scheduling link-level entanglement and creating task-specific multipartite entanglement.
AI.method: Formulates a Markov Decision Process and trains policies with double deep Q-networks (DQN) combined with Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs), experience replay buffers, and curriculum training; key physical parameter is link activation probability. Also explores interpretability via metrics and by tasking an LLM to derive a novel heuristic from example actions of the trained policy.
AI.result: Policies maintain 100% success for up to 71% lower link activation probability than baselines on physically relevant topologies; under hardware-type placement restrictions, they maintain at least 80% success for up to 59% lower link activation probability. The LLM-derived heuristic performs similarly to the DQN policy.
AI.conclusion: RL with graph neural networks yields resource-efficient entanglement scheduling policies, and LLM-based heuristic extraction offers a promising interpretable alternative for large quantum networks where direct training is computationally expensive.
